title: Lesson 3: Double Fast, Half Fast - Multiplication Secrets
learningGoals: Double and halve any 2-digit number mentally using the Anurupyena (proportionality) sutra.
Multiply by 4 by doubling twice and by 8 by doubling three times.
Recognise the doubling chain as a proportional shortcut that scales to x16 and beyond.
coreIdeas: Every multiplication by 4 is just doubling twice - no new skill needed.
Multiplying by 8 means doubling three times in a row, each step quick and exact.
Halving is the reverse of doubling - knowing both gives you a full proportional toolkit.

workedExamples.question: Half of 84 = ?
workedExamples.method: Half of 80 = 40. Half of 4 = 2. Total = 42. Answer: 42.

starterPractice: Double 37 using the split method (double tens + double units).
Halve 96. Then halve the result. What did you just compute?

onboarding.coachIntro: Today you will use doubling and halving like number tools, so multiplying by 4, 8, and even 16 feels simple and fast.
onboarding.placementRule: Start at group A. If the learner can double any 2-digit number instantly, skip to group D.

mission.missionPromise: Lock in quick doubles first, then turn that same move into x4, x8, and x16 answers.
mission.successCelebration: Well done. You can now use doubling to handle x4, x8, and x16 with much less effort.

microLessonPattern: Coach shows one doubling step with a visual chain.
Board highlights how each double leads to the next.
Student practises one doubling step before seeing the chain completed.
Instant feedback shows which step in the chain was wrong.
Review prompt asks the student to write the full chain for a new number.

rewardLoop.xpUnit: Award 10 to 18 XP per exercise group based on difficulty.
rewardLoop.streakRule: Keep the streak counter visible; a correct answer on retry still counts as streak-save.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Each group earns a themed badge tied to the doubling skill being practised.
rewardLoop.celebrationStyle: Short coach cheer, XP pulse animation, and progress bar moves forward.

reviewLoop.trigger: Two wrong answers in one group triggers a mini re-teach with a simpler number.
reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Re-show the doubling chain, then give a smaller number to try.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance only after the student answers the checkpoint correctly.
reviewLoop.revisitRule: Missed groups reappear at the start of the next session as warm-up cards.

uiDirectives.noScrollGoal: Student sees mission progress, question card, and action buttons without scrolling.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Before we race ahead, we need one strong move. If you can double a number in one look, the rest of this lesson becomes easy.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Flash a short doubles ladder: 3 to 6, 4 to 8, 5 to 10, 7 to 14, 9 to 18. Show each as two equal groups making one quick total.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Now answer quickly: what is double 9?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. That is the quick doubling move we will keep using.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Think of two 9s together: 9 + 9 = 18. So double 9 is 18.

sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Double-double done! That is x4 without any times table memorisation.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: For 17 x 4: double 17=34, double 34=68. Two quick steps!

screenplay.teacherLine: Doubling is the key move behind multiplying by 4, 8, and 16. Let us start with the basics.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Think of doubling as adding the number to itself.

visual.title: Single-digit doubles
visual.caption: Build instant recall by spotting each double on the chain.

screenplay.teacherLine: Here is the secret - x4 is just double, then double again! Watch: 23 ? 46 ? 92. That is 23 x 4!

visual.title: Multiply by 4
visual.caption: Double once, then double again to get x4.

screenplay.teacherLine: Watch the doubles chain: 3 becomes 6, 4 becomes 8, 5 becomes 10, 7 becomes 14, 9 becomes 18. Each is just the number added to itself — instant!
screenplay.fallbackHint: Add the number to itself to double it.

visual.title: Single-digit doubles — Demo
visual.caption: Watch the doubles chain: 3→6, 4→8, 5→10...

screenplay.teacherLine: Together: double 6. Add 6 to itself. 6 + 6 = ?
Watch: double 34. Split into 30 and 4. Double 30 = 60. Double 4 = 8. Add: 60 + 8 = 68. Two tiny steps — done!
screenplay.boardAction: Show split: 34 → 30+4. Double each: 60+8. Combine: 68. Box the answer.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Double tens and units separately, then add.

visual.title: Split and double — Demo
visual.caption: Double 34: split → double each → combine.

screenplay.teacherLine: Together: double 47. Double 40 = 80. Double 7 = 14. What is 80 + 14?
screenplay.boardAction: Show: double 40=80, double 7=14. Wait for sum. Reveal 94.

screenplay.teacherLine: Watch: half of 84. Split into 80 and 4. Half of 80 = 40. Half of 4 = 2. Add: 40 + 2 = 42. Halving is doubling in reverse!
screenplay.boardAction: Show: half 84 → half 80=40, half 4=2. Combine: 42. Box the answer.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Halve the tens and units separately, then add.

screenplay.teacherLine: Together: half of 68. Half of 60 = 30. Half of 8 = 4. What is 30 + 4?
Watch: 24 × 4. Step 1 — double 24 = 48. Step 2 — double 48 = 96. Answer: 96. Two doublings and you are done — no table memorisation needed!
screenplay.fallbackHint: Double the number, then double again.

visual.title: Multiply by 4 — Demo
visual.caption: 24 × 4: double 24=48, double 48=96.

screenplay.teacherLine: Together: 16 × 4. First double 16 = 32. Now double 32 = ?

visual.title: Guided: 16 × 4
visual.caption: Double 16=32, double 32 = ?

screenplay.teacherLine: Watch: 15 × 8. Three doublings: 15 → 30 → 60 → 120. Each arrow is just doubling. Answer: 120!
Together: 14 × 8. Double 14 = 28. Double 28 = 56. Double 56 = ?
Detective mode: 14 × 8. Options: 104, 108, 112, 116. Build chain: 14 → 28 → 56 → 112. I circle 112. The wrong options are close but off by 4 — the chain never lies!
screenplay.boardAction: Show four options. Build chain 14→28→56→112. Circle 112. Cross out others.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Build the doubling chain to get the exact product, then match.

visual.title: Spot the product — Demo
visual.caption: Build chain 14→28→56→112.

screenplay.teacherLine: Together: 13 × 4. Double 13 = 26. Double 26 = ?

visual.title: Guided: 13 × 4
visual.caption: Double 13=26, double 26 = ?

screenplay.teacherLine: Watch: 13 × 8 step by step. Box 1: 13 × 2 = 26. Box 2: 26 × 2 = 52. Box 3: 52 × 2 = 104. Three boxes, three doublings — answer 104!
screenplay.boardAction: Show three boxes: [26] [52] [104] with ×2 arrows. Label each step.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Fill each box by doubling the previous result.

screenplay.teacherLine: Together: 17 × 8. Step 1: double 17 = 34. Step 2: double 34 = 68. Step 3: double 68 = ?
Mixed problems! 32 × 4: double-double → 32 → 64 → 128. Half of 52: split 50+2, halve each → 25+1 = 26. Pick the right tool for each!
screenplay.boardAction: Show 32×4 chain (double-double) and half of 52 (split-halve) side by side with labels.
screenplay.fallbackHint: Use doubling chain for ×4 or ×8. Use split-halve for halving.

visual.title: Mixed drill — Demo
visual.caption: Two methods side by side — pick the right one.

screenplay.teacherLine: Together: half of 72. Half of 70 = 35. Half of 2 = 1. What is 35 + 1?
Watch: 18 × 16. Four doublings: 18 → 36 → 72 → 144 → 288. One extra double after ×8 and you have ×16!
screenplay.boardAction: Show four-step chain: 18→36→72→144→288 with ×2 arrows. Box 288.

screenplay.teacherLine: Together: 11 × 16. Chain: 11 → 22 → 44 → 88 → ___. What is the last doubling?
